X-rays of patient no. 1 showing dysostosis multiplex at ends of long bones and vertebrae

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Frontal clinical photo of patient no. 1 at 9 months with caption explicitly attributing coarse facial features, long philtrum, tower skull and short neck to ML II (mucolipidosis type II); classic coarse facies of the target disease. B: Intraoral clinical photo of the same 9-month-old patient no. 1 with caption stating hypertrophic gingiva, matching the vocabulary finding of gingival hyperplasia in ML II; visible perioral skin is light. C: Skeletal radiographs (chest, long bones, spine, skull) of the same 9-month-old patient no. 1 with caption explicitly describing dysostosis multiplex, the classic radiologic manifestation of ML II; no skin visible so skin_tone is null.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Human patient radiograph of a 21-month-old girl explicitly stated to have ML II; bullet-shaped broad under-modelled proximal phalanges and pointed metacarpals are textbook dysostosis multiplex of I-cell disease. b: Human patient radiograph of the same ML II case; iliac/femoral dysplasia with resorption and crook deformity are classic dysostosis multiplex features of mucolipidosis type II. c: Human patient radiograph of the same ML II case; anterior vertebral beaking with thoracolumbar kyphosis is a textbook dysostosis multiplex sign explicitly listed in the vocabulary. d: Human patient skull radiograph of the same ML II case; J-shaped sella turcica is a classic skeletal-survey component of dysostosis multiplex in mucolipidosis type II, with the specific sign added as a proposed finding.

The proximal metacarpals show a mixture of features of osteodystrophy and dysostosis multiplex, becoming eroded and narrowed to a point. The carpal bones are osteopenic and hypoplastic. panels.rationale: Day 1 left-leg radiograph from Patient 1 with Mucolipidosis Type II (I-Cell Disease). Caption explicitly attributes diaphyseal cloaking and talocalcaneal stippling (white arrow) as feature of I-cell disease, matching vocabulary finding for periosteal cloaking.
panels.attribution_text: Boruah et al. Secondary Hyperparathyroidism in Children with Mucolipidosis Type II (I-Cell Disease): Irish Experience.. Journal of clinical medicine 2022. doi:10.3390/jcm11051366. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Acute findings of hyperparathyroidism and rickets. Patient 1, left leg radiograph day 1 demonstrates features of hyperparathyroidism including reduced bone density, subperiosteal resorption and poor cortical delineation (see medial tibia) as well as diaphyseal cloaking of the femur and tibia (arrowheads). Features of rickets are seen with cupped, splayed and frayed metaphyses especially in the distal femur. Diaphyseal angulation consistent with antenatal fractures is seen in the distal femur and tibia. Additionally, talocalcaneal stippling, a feature of I-cell disease is also present (white arrow).
in_text_mentions: Skeletal radiographs in the first week of life were available for four patients and at 2 months of age for one patient (Patient 3). Follow up radiographs were available for four out five patients. Early radiographs already showed marked changes of hyperparathyroidism in all five infants including osteopenia, subperiosteal resorption, poor cortical delineation, periosteal new bone formation with ‘cloaking’ (linear periosteal new bone parallel to the shaft of the bone but widely separated from the bone), metaphyseal irregularity and submetaphyseal lucent bands (Figure 1 and Figure 2).

All early radiographs also showed features of rickets, with metaphyseal cupping, fraying and splaying (Figure 1 and Figure 2). There was evidence of antenatal long bone fractures in Patients 1, 2 and 4. Patient 4 also had an acute fracture of the proximal left humeral neck (Figure 3). Further radiographic findings of ML II including talocalcaneal stippling were identified in Patients 1, 2 and 5, and an abnormal appearance of the vertebral bodies with increased height; rounding and sclerosis were seen in Patients 1, 2 and 4.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Lateral spine radiograph in article titled mucolipidosis II with caption describing kyphosis and developmental abnormality and in-text stating characteristic skeletal dysplasia, consistent with dysostosis multiplex. B: Hand/wrist radiograph with captioned abnormal cartilage development in mucolipidosis II case, part of skeletal dysplasia / dysostosis multiplex spectrum. C: Axial chest CT with captioned chest deformity in mucolipidosis II patient, consistent with dysostosis multiplex; interstitial lung changes captioned but not in vocabulary so in proposed findings.

panels.figure_caption: (A) The x-ray shows the spine have kyphosis at the junction of the thoracolumbar segment. Thoracic and lumbar physiological curvature developmental abnormalities. (B) The cartilage development of wrist joint was abnormal. (C) The chest was deformed and the interstitial changes of the lungs were obvious.
in_text_mentions: The results of biochemical tests and routine blood, bowel and urine tests were all negative. Characteristic features of skeletal dysplasia were observed in vertebral side x-ray imaging (Figure 3). A cranial CT scan showed ventriculomegaly and abnormal skull development (Figure 4). Echocardiography revealed that the foramen ovale was patent, and the EF was normal. The development screening test (DST) showed that the patient's mental and motor development were significantly delayed (Table 1).
